title: Chapter 1 Mastery Quiz: Neurons, Glia & Neural Communication
description: Test your mastery of cellular neuroscience, resting potentials, action potentials, synaptic transmission, and neurotransmitters.

questions.question: What is the primary function of dendritic spines on a multipolar neuron?

options.text: To insulate the axon against electrical leakage
To increase surface area and receive synaptic inputs from other neurons
To package neurotransmitters into synaptic vesicles
To synthesize ATP in the mitochondrial matrix

questions.explanation: Dendritic spines provide specialized chemical micro-compartments that vastly expand the receptive surface area for presynaptic inputs.

questions.question: Which glial cell type forms the protective myelin sheath around axons within the peripheral nervous system (PNS)?

options.text: Oligodendrocytes
Schwann cells
Astrocytes
Ependymal cells

questions.explanation: Schwann cells myelinate individual axonal segments in the PNS, whereas oligodendrocytes myelinate multiple axons in the CNS.

questions.question: Microglia are best characterized as:

options.text: The primary electrical insulators of motor nerves
The resident immune cells and phagocytes of the central nervous system
Producers of cerebrospinal fluid in brain ventricles
Structural support cells maintaining the blood-brain barrier

questions.explanation: Microglia function as specialized phagocytes that engulf cellular debris, pathogens, and prune synapses.

questions.question: What is the typical value of a mammalian neuron's resting membrane potential?

options.text: +40 mV
0 mV
-70 mV
-55 mV

questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential is typically approximately -70 mV, indicating that the interior of the cell is negative relative to the outside.

questions.question: The sodium-potassium ATPase pump transports ions in which direction across the cell membrane?

options.text: 3 Na+ ions out of the cell for every 2 K+ ions pumped into the cell
2 Na+ ions out of the cell for every 3 K+ ions pumped into the cell
3 Na+ ions into the cell for every 2 K+ ions pumped out of the cell
2 Na+ ions into the cell for every 2 K+ ions pumped out of the cell

questions.explanation: The sodium-potassium pump moves 3 Na+ ions outward and 2 K+ ions inward against their concentration gradients using ATP.

questions.question: At resting potential (-70 mV), what forces act on Sodium (Na+) ions?

options.text: Both concentration gradient and electrical gradient push Na+ into the cell
Concentration gradient pushes Na+ out, but electrical gradient pulls it in
Concentration gradient pushes Na+ in, but electrical gradient repels it out
Neither gradient exerts any force on Na+ at rest

questions.explanation: Na+ is at higher concentration outside and the cell interior is negative, so both diffusion and electrostatic pressure drive Na+ inward.

questions.question: What is meant by the 'All-or-None Law' of action potentials?

options.text: All neurons in a tract must fire at the exact same moment
Once threshold is reached, an action potential fires at complete, invariant amplitude
A neuron either releases all its neurotransmitter vesicles or none at all
Action potentials only occur when all glial cells are active

questions.explanation: The All-or-None Law states that an action potential occurs at full magnitude or not at all; it does not grade in amplitude with stimulus strength.

questions.question: During which phase of the action potential do voltage-gated potassium (K+) channels open while sodium channels inactivate?

options.text: Depolarization
Repolarization
Resting state
Spatial summation

questions.explanation: Repolarization occurs when voltage-gated Na+ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K+ channels open, allowing K+ to exit the cell.

questions.question: Why is it physiologically impossible to trigger another action potential during the absolute refractory period?

options.text: Voltage-gated sodium channels are locked in an inactivated state
The cell has completely run out of intracellular ATP
The myelin sheath has temporarily dissolved
Neurotransmitter vesicles are completely exhausted

questions.explanation: During the absolute refractory period, voltage-gated Na+ channels are inactivated and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes.

questions.question: How does myelin accelerate the transmission speed of action potentials?

options.text: By allowing continuous opening of sodium channels at every point on the axon
By forcing action potentials to regenerate only at the unmyelinated Nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction)
By increasing the temperature of the axon
By converting electrical signals into magnetic waves

questions.explanation: Saltatory conduction allows the depolarization to travel passively beneath the myelin sheath, jumping from one node of Ranvier to the next.

questions.question: What is the critical ion that triggers the exocytosis of synaptic vesicles at the presynaptic terminal?

options.text: Chloride (Cl-)
Calcium (Ca2+)
Magnesium (Mg2+)
Potassium (K+)

questions.explanation: Depolarization of the presynaptic terminal opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels; Ca2+ influx triggers SNARE proteins to fuse vesicles with the membrane.

questions.question: In comparison to ionotropic receptors, metabotropic receptors are characterized by:

options.text: Direct ion channel pore opening in under 1 millisecond
Coupling to intracellular G-proteins that activate secondary messenger cascades
Resistance to any chemical modulation or drug binding
Being located exclusively on glial cell membranes

questions.explanation: Metabotropic receptors operate via G-proteins and second messenger systems, producing slower, longer-lasting, and more widespread modulatory effects.

questions.question: An Excitatory Postsynaptic Potential (EPSP) typically results from the opening of which ion channels?

options.text: Sodium (Na+) channels allowing positive ions to enter
Chloride (Cl-) channels allowing negative ions to enter
Potassium (K+) channels allowing positive ions to leave
Calcium channels pumping Ca2+ out of the neuron

questions.explanation: EPSPs are depolarizing graded potentials caused primarily by the inward flow of positively charged sodium (Na+) ions.

questions.question: An Inhibitory Postsynaptic Potential (IPSP) hyperpolarizes a neuron by which mechanism?

options.text: Allowing chloride (Cl-) influx or potassium (K+) efflux
Allowing rapid sodium (Na+) influx
Inactivating all glial astrocytes
Blocking the sodium-potassium pump

questions.explanation: Entry of negative Cl- ions or exit of positive K+ ions makes the intracellular voltage more negative, driving the neuron further from threshold.

questions.question: What is spatial summation in neuronal integration?

options.text: The addition of post-synaptic potentials from multiple different synapses occurring at the same time
The addition of potentials triggered in rapid succession at a single synapse
The growth of new dendritic spines over weeks
The elimination of inactive synapses by microglia

questions.explanation: Spatial summation occurs when inputs from multiple distinct synapses across the dendritic arbor converge at the axon hillock simultaneously.

questions.question: What is the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the mammalian central nervous system?

options.text: GABA
Glutamate
Glycine
Serotonin

questions.explanation: Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain, binding to AMPA, NMDA, and kainate receptors.

questions.question: Which neurotransmitter is primarily synthesized in the Substantia Nigra and Ventral Tegmental Area (VTA)?

options.text: Dopamine
Serotonin
Acetylcholine
Histamine

questions.explanation: Dopaminergic cell bodies are concentrated in the substantia nigra (motor control) and VTA (reward and motivation).

questions.question: Degeneration of cholinergic neurons originating in the basal forebrain (nucleus basalis of Meynert) is strongly correlated with:

options.text: Huntington's chorea
Alzheimer's disease
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
Bipolar disorder

questions.explanation: Acetylcholine loss in the basal forebrain pathways is a prominent neuropathological hallmark of Alzheimer's disease.

questions.question: What happens when an enzyme inhibitor blocks Acetylcholinesterase (AChE)?

options.text: Acetylcholine cannot be synthesized
Acetylcholine accumulates and continuously stimulates postsynaptic receptors
Axons fail to develop myelin sheaths
GABA receptors are permanently locked shut

questions.explanation: AChE breaks down acetylcholine; inhibiting it prevents degradation, causing acetylcholine to linger and overstimulate cholinergic receptors.

questions.question: Which of the following describes an 'antagonist' in psychopharmacology?

options.text: A drug that binds to a receptor and blocks or diminishes its normal physiological action
A drug that mimics the endogenous ligand to trigger a maximal response
A molecule that accelerates the reuptake of neurotransmitters
A hormone secreted by the pineal gland to induce sleep

questions.explanation: Antagonists bind to receptors with high affinity but lack intrinsic efficacy, thereby preventing endogenous neurotransmitters from binding.

questions.question: What is 'excitotoxicity' in the nervous system?

options.text: Neuronal injury or death resulting from excessive glutamate stimulation and calcium overload
Excessive dopamine release causing auditory hallucinations
Complete absence of action potentials in sensory neurons
The rapid proliferation of cancerous glial cells

questions.explanation: Excessive glutamate overactivates NMDA receptors, allowing toxic amounts of Ca2+ into neurons, which activates destructive catabolic enzymes.

questions.question: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) increase serotonergic transmission primarily by:

options.text: Directly activating postsynaptic 5-HT1A receptors
Blocking the presynaptic serotonin transporter protein (SERT)
Accelerating serotonin enzymatic breakdown by MAO
Stimulating dopamine synthesis in the substantia nigra

questions.explanation: SSRIs inhibit SERT, preventing reuptake and keeping serotonin in the synaptic cleft longer to bind postsynaptic receptors.
